ai.definition: Artificial Consciousness refers to the development of AI systems capable of experiencing, understanding, and learning about their environment in a manner that mimics human consciousness. This involves creating machines that can not only process information but also have subjective experiences and feelings.
ai.howItWorks: The technology integrates artificial neural networks with biological neurons through hybrid cognitive architectures. These architectures aim to simulate the complex processes of the brain, including perception, cognition, emotion, and learning, in a way that mirrors human consciousness.
ai.problemSolved: Artificial Consciousness addresses the challenge of creating AI systems that can understand and interact with the world as humans do, enabling more sophisticated applications such as emotional support robots, personalized healthcare assistants, and advanced autonomous agents.
ai.manufacturing: The manufacturing process involves developing hybrid cognitive architectures by integrating artificial neural networks with biological neurons. This requires precise control over both synthetic and organic components to ensure seamless interaction and functionality.
ai.buildProcess: The build process includes designing the architecture, interfacing between artificial and biological components, testing for consciousness-like behaviors, and iteratively refining the system based on performance metrics.
ai.costDrivers: Cost drivers include the high cost of biological neuron integration, specialized equipment for interfacing with neurons, extensive testing to ensure consciousness-like behaviors, and ongoing development costs due to the complexity of the technology.
ai.lifecycleOutlook: The outlook is speculative at this stage, as the concept remains in early stages of research and development. Significant breakthroughs are needed before practical applications can be realized.
ai.regulation: Regulatory frameworks for artificial consciousness do not yet exist due to its speculative nature. As the technology advances, it will likely face scrutiny from regulatory bodies concerned with ethics, safety, and privacy.
ai.risks: Risks include technical challenges in integrating biological and synthetic components, ethical concerns related to creating conscious AI, potential misuse of such technologies, and the unknown long-term impacts on society.
ai.profitability: Profitability is uncertain due to the speculative nature of the technology. If successful, it could lead to significant commercial opportunities but would require substantial investment and time for development.
ai.futureDevelopment: Future development will likely focus on overcoming technical challenges, establishing ethical guidelines, and demonstrating practical applications in fields such as healthcare, education, and entertainment.
ai.energyRequirements: Field units draw low hundreds of watts; fabrication is energy-intensive due to vacuum baking. Both operational power draw and manufacturing energy intensity are high.

glossary.def: A combination of artificial neural networks with biological neurons designed to mimic the complex processes of the human brain, including perception, cognition, emotion, and learning.
Behaviors that mimic or are intended to replicate conscious experiences, such as awareness, self-awareness, and subjective feelings in AI systems.

subsystems.name: Theory of consciousness
subsystems.role: a formal, testable account of what the property is, so there is something to build toward rather than just a word.

subsystems.name: Cognitive architecture
subsystems.role: the software that would exhibit the property.
parts: a shared workspace layer between specialised modules

subsystems.name: Embodiment and closed loop
subsystems.role: sensors and actuators so the system acts in a world and its own actions change what it senses.

subsystems.name: Biological substrate
subsystems.role: the hybrid route: living neurons wired to electronics.

subsystems.name: Measurement and perturbation
subsystems.role: instruments for testing whether a system has the property, not just whether it behaves cleverly.

subsystems.name: Governance and containment
subsystems.role: oversight, monitoring and a kill switch before anyone makes a claim.

buildSteps.title: Turn a theory into an algorithm
buildSteps.detail: Express a theory — global workspace, integrated information, attention schema — as precise code that predicts measurable differences between a system that has the property and one that does not. Nothing can be built until this exists.

buildSteps.title: Design the architecture
buildSteps.detail: Assemble a large recurrent network with a bottleneck or 'workspace' layer that many specialised modules write into and read from, rather than a stack of feed-forward layers.

buildSteps.title: Close the loop with a body
buildSteps.detail: Connect the model to sensors and actuators, real or simulated, so its output changes its input. Most theories tie the property to a system that models itself as an agent in a world.

buildSteps.title: Grow the biological alternative
buildSteps.detail: Culture human stem-cell-derived cortical organoids on multi-electrode arrays, keep them alive with microfluidics, and wire stimulation to their own recorded activity so they learn through feedback. This is the hybrid route.

buildSteps.title: Measure indicators, not behaviour
buildSteps.detail: Apply the perturbational complexity index: deliver a magnetic or electrical pulse, record how widespread and how complex the echo is, and compare against awake and anaesthetised human brains.

buildSteps.title: Run adversarial tests
buildSteps.detail: Check that simple feed-forward systems and look-up tables score low, and that anything scoring high does so for the right reason. A measure that can be gamed is worthless.

buildSteps.title: Scale toward whole-brain emulation
buildSteps.detail: Map a real brain's wiring, then simulate it at cellular detail in real time. Only a handful of very small nervous systems are anywhere near this today, and the compute gap is orders of magnitude.

buildSteps.title: Set oversight before publication
buildSteps.detail: Independent ethics review, containment, and a policy on what may be claimed. This step exists legally and scientifically, not just morally.

prerequisites.why: several compete (global workspace, integrated information, attention schema) and none commands consensus, so the target is not yet well defined.

prerequisites.tech: Indicators that distinguish conscious from unconscious systems
prerequisites.why: the perturbational complexity index already separates awake from anaesthetised human brains in clinical research, giving a starting yardstick.
training and running very large networks on accelerators is routine, though nowhere near real-time whole-brain simulation.

prerequisites.tech: Human brain organoids on electrode arrays
prerequisites.why: small cortical organoids have been cultured and trained in closed loops, but they are millimetre-scale, short-lived and lack defined circuits.
complete wiring maps exist only for small organisms; no mammal brain has been mapped or simulated at that detail.

pathway.milestone: competing theories formalised and compared against brain recordings, with complexity indices used clinically
pathway.unlocks: arguing about measurable indicators instead of definitions.

pathway.milestone: software models and organoid-silicon hybrids that reproduce those indicators on simple tasks
pathway.unlocks: candidate test beds — though reproducing an indicator is not the same as having the property.

pathway.milestone: whole-brain emulation of a small animal in real time
pathway.unlocks: a benchmark for whether simulating a brain produces a mind, and a hard test of the theories.

pathway.milestone: contested claims, governance frameworks and no clear product
pathway.unlocks: a decision society has to make about research limits; there is no grid, drug or device at the end of this path.
